name: Facial lifting tape
lead: Facial lifting tape consists of adhesive strips or clear patches that are stuck to the cheeks, jawline or temples and pulled back, usually hidden under hair, to make sagging skin look tighter and the jawline and cheekbones look more defined. People use it for photographs, filming and events because the change is visible immediately and needs no procedure. The practice has a long history in photography, film and event styling.

The lift is mechanical: the adhesive holds the skin in a different position while the tape is worn, so the effect is expected to end when the tape comes off. No published study has examined cosmetic lifting tape for skin structure or lasting effect. Published research on facial taping concerns other uses, including elastic therapeutic tape for swelling after facial fracture surgery and taping as part of rehabilitation for Bell's palsy.[1][2]

For context, surgical facelifts (rhytidectomy) have a history stretching back to about 1901, and Wikipedia describes skin-only facelifts as lasting roughly five to ten years, with costs in the thousands of dollars; tape is positioned by users as a short-term, low-cost alternative for specific occasions.[4] Reported drawbacks of tape include skin irritation and adhesive reactions.

chain: Adhesive strip anchors to skin at cheek or jaw
Pulled toward hairline or behind the ear and hidden
Skin looks tauter and the jaw and cheeks look more defined while worn
angle.text: The tape visibly pulls loose skin back for the duration it is worn, which is why it is used for photos, video and events. The change is cosmetic and temporary, ending when the tape is removed.

infobox: Elastic therapeutic (kinesiology) tape, developed 1970s by Kenzo Kase [5]
Adhesive skin irritation and allergic contact dermatitis [6]

paras: Products include clear or skin-tone adhesive patches, pre-cut strips with a pull-tab and elastic bands attached to medical-grade tape. The user places the adhesive on the skin of the cheek or jaw, pulls the loose end toward the hairline or behind the ear and fixes it, and conceals the ends with hair. Stylists and makeup artists have used such techniques for decades.

The usual target areas are the jawline and jowls, the cheeks and mid-face, the corners of the eyes and the area around the temples, because hair or a hairstyle can cover the anchor points there. Some kits pair the tape with small hooks or elastic bands that connect the two sides behind the head, and some are sold as clear stickers meant to be worn under makeup.

Lifting tape works by direct traction on the skin. It does not stimulate collagen or change tissue, so any change in appearance lasts only as long as the tape stays in place. A separate category, elastic therapeutic (kinesio) tape, is applied in sports and rehabilitation medicine, where proponents claim effects on swelling and circulation; one 2018 randomized study of 28 men found that applying kinesio tape with wrinkles (convolutions) on the lower back did not increase skin temperature, which the authors used as a proxy for local circulation.[3]

Tape and adhesive devices for pulling the face taut have a long association with photography, film and television styling, where makeup artists and stylists use them out of frame for a tighter look on camera, as commonly described. Surgical facelifting has a documented history reaching back to about 1901, and tape is positioned alongside it as a reversible, short-term option.[4]

Wikipedia divides the history of the surgical facelift into a cutaneous period (1900 to 1970), in which surgeons pulled the skin and cut away the excess, a period in the 1970s when Tord Skoog introduced deeper dissection and Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS layer in 1976, a deep-plane period in the 1980s, and a volumetric period since 1991 that emphasises restoring volume.[4] Skin tension was therefore the original mechanism of the surgical lift, which is the same principle that tape applies temporarily from outside.

The related category of elastic therapeutic or kinesio tape was developed in the 1970s by the Japanese-American chiropractor Kenzo Kase and gained mass visibility when it was supplied to athletes at the 2008 Beijing and 2012 London Olympics, with beach volleyball player Kerri Walsh's shoulder tape credited with bringing it to public attention.[5] Cosmetic lifting tape borrows the idea of an adhesive strip applied to skin under tension, although it is a different product designed for a different purpose.

Lifting tape is discussed as an instant, low-cost way to look more defined for photographs, video calls, dates or events. The usual appeal is that the effect is immediate, reversible and can be adjusted, which makes it a counterpart to makeup contouring and to styling tools such as hairstyles that hide the anchor points.

Some users also apply tape at night in the hope of lasting effects. Whether overnight use has any lasting effect has not been studied. A related and separate product category is nightly wrinkle patches, which are marketed to smooth lines such as forehead and chest creases rather than to lift the jawline.

A 2016 review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal by Anson, Kane and Lambros discussed how wrinkles arise from expression and from mechanical forces during sleep; it reported that side or stomach sleeping puts compression and shear on the face, and that sleep compression may contribute to skin expansion as well as to wrinkling.[7] This is the background to products that hold the skin flat overnight, although the review is about the mechanism of sleep wrinkles and does not evaluate tape.

Adhesives are discussed in dermatology under contact dermatitis. Wikipedia describes irritant contact dermatitis as the most common type, about 80 percent of cases, with burning and dry or fissured skin at the contact site, and allergic contact dermatitis as a delayed reaction appearing 24 to 72 hours after exposure with itching and sometimes blisters. It lists acrylates among known allergens and notes that rashes usually fade over days to weeks once contact stops [6]. Elastic therapeutic tape uses a heat-activated acrylic adhesive [5].

Wikipedia summarises several meta-analyses of elastic therapeutic tape in sport and musculoskeletal pain, reporting trivial pain relief in a 2012 analysis, negligible effects on strength in 2014, and short-term pain reduction in chronic low back pain in a later review, with critics arguing that benefits may reflect placebo effects [5]. These findings concern body use, not facial lifting.
No studies found of adhesive facial lifting tape for cosmetic skin lifting or anti-aging.

subs.h: Related research on taping of the face
paras: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials (319 participants) examined elastic therapeutic tape after surgery for facial fractures. Only two trials were suitable for pooling edema data, and the authors concluded that tape appeared effective for controlling postoperative edema, with unclear effects on pain and trismus and a high risk of bias in the included studies.[1]

A randomized study of 20 patients with Bell's palsy examined facial taping as a biofeedback aid alongside Kabat rehabilitation, and reported greater improvement in palsy severity scores in the taping group than with rehabilitation alone.[2] These applications address swelling or neuromuscular rehabilitation rather than cosmetic lifting.

Adhesives can cause contact irritation, allergic reactions and redness or stripping of the skin on removal, and wearing tape overnight or for long periods can leave marks. No studies have quantified these risks for cosmetic lifting tape.

The facial skin is thinner than skin on the limbs, and the eyelids and temples are particularly delicate, so people with sensitive skin or known adhesive allergies are generally told by dermatology sources that irritant and allergic contact dermatitis are the main adhesive hazards.[6]

Wikipedia's article on rhytidectomy traces the surgical facelift from 1901 and describes later developments such as SMAS-layer techniques (1976) and deep plane and volumetric approaches. It reports that skin-only facelifts can last about five to ten years and that recovery for a traditional facelift is around three to four weeks.[4]

The same article lists non-surgical options including thread lifts, which it describes as using barbed threads to pull skin upward; it quotes physician Vincent Wong in a 2021 BBC report calling thread lifts the most dangerous procedure an aesthetic practitioner can do. It does not discuss tape.[4] Tape differs from these in that it involves no tissue change and is fully reversible.

Tape sits alongside other instant appearance aids such as makeup contouring, hairstyles that conceal anchor points, and posture and lighting choices for photographs. Longer-term approaches that people discuss for facial firmness include skincare, microcurrent devices, facial exercise, injectables and surgical lifts; Wikipedia lists microcurrent treatment under non-surgical facelift options.[4]

timeline.event: Eugen Holländer reportedly performs the first facelift in Berlin.[4]
Kenzo Kase develops elastic therapeutic tape; Tord Skoog introduces deeper facelift dissection.[5][4]
Mitz and Peyronie describe the SMAS layer, shaping modern facelift techniques.[4]
Start of the volumetric period of facelift surgery, per Wikipedia.[4]
Elastic therapeutic tape gains public visibility at the Beijing Olympics.[5]
Elastic tape further popularised at the London Olympics; early meta-analyses of its effects appear.[5]
Anson, Kane and Lambros review mechanical sleep wrinkles in Aesthetic Surgery Journal.[7]
Randomized study finds kinesio tape applied with convolutions did not raise skin temperature.[3]
Randomized study of facial taping as biofeedback in Bell's palsy published.[2]
Meta-analysis of elastic therapeutic tape after facial fracture surgery published.[1]

lore.intro: Lifting tape is discussed mainly as a photo-day or event styling trick, with some users also asking whether wearing it at night can tighten skin over time.

claims.claim: Tape gives an instant lifted jawline for photos
claims.believers: Users and sellers say strips hidden under hair give a more defined jaw and cheek for the duration of an event or shoot.
claims.experts: The mechanism is direct traction on the skin, so the effect lasts while the tape is worn; no study has measured cosmetic lifting tape.

claims.claim: Wearing tape overnight trains the skin to stay lifted
claims.believers: Some users say that repeated overnight use leaves skin firmer.
claims.experts: No published study has examined this for facial lifting tape; research on taping of the face concerns post-surgical swelling and Bell's palsy rehabilitation.[1][2]

claims.claim: Taping boosts circulation under the skin
claims.believers: Elastic tape manufacturers have claimed that lifting the skin improves lymphatic flow.[5]
claims.experts: A 2018 randomized study of 28 men found that kinesio tape applied with convolutions did not raise skin temperature, used as a circulation proxy.[3]

claims.claim: Tape is a safe, reversible substitute for a facelift
claims.believers: Users point to the lack of surgery, cost and downtime compared with a surgical lift.
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes surgical facelifts as lasting years with weeks of recovery and tissue changes, whereas tape works only while worn; the main reported tape hazards are adhesive skin reactions.[4][6]

claims.claim: Holding the skin flat during sleep prevents sleep wrinkles
claims.believers: Sellers of overnight patches say keeping skin flat reduces lines caused by sleep position.
claims.experts: A 2016 review described sleep compression and shear as contributors to facial wrinkling, but it did not evaluate tape or patches.[7]

claims.claim: Elastic tape works on the face the way it does for athletes
claims.believers: Proponents of kinesio taping say it supports tissue and swelling.[5]
claims.experts: A 2024 meta-analysis found tape appeared effective for postoperative edema after facial fracture surgery with high risk of bias, while body-use meta-analyses report trivial to short-term effects.[1][5]
